turns.speaker: Pravalika Reddy
turns.text: Thanks everyone for joining the Q4 core architecture sync. Today we need a definitive decision on our distributed caching layer. Our current Memcached cluster is hitting hot-shard limits during morning spikes.

turns.speaker: Marcus Vance
turns.text: The primary issue is p99 latency climbing past 450 milliseconds whenever three enterprise clients sync their calendar indexes simultaneously. I evaluated two proposals: upgrading our Memcached topology with consistent hashing, versus migrating to a multi-node Redis cluster with active read replicas.

turns.speaker: Dave Kowalski
turns.text: From an SRE perspective, operating standalone Memcached instances across three AWS availability zones has caused intermittent split-brain scenarios when VPC peering drops. Redis 7 with failover automation would reduce our on-call risk significantly.

turns.speaker: Pravalika Reddy
turns.text: Given the reliability concerns, I'm leaning toward Redis 7 with Raft consensus for the session tier.

turns.speaker: Sarah Lin
turns.text: I agree, but we need to make sure the migration doesn't introduce data consistency problems during the transition.

turns.speaker: Marcus Vance
turns.text: Then we should explicitly reject write-behind caching and use dual-write shadow traffic during the migration.

turns.speaker: Pravalika Reddy
turns.text: Agreed. We'll start with a 10 percent canary, monitor the failover benchmarks, and expand over two sprints.

turns.speaker: Dave Kowalski
turns.text: That gives SRE a clear rollback path and removes the current single-cluster failure concern.

turns.speaker: Pravalika Reddy
turns.text: Let's record the decision: Redis 7 cluster migration, no write-behind caching, and a phased dual-write rollout.
